newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - PPI due, markets seen buoyant.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - PPI due, markets seen buoyant.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets a handful of economic reports on Friday, none of which should spoil the market's upbeat tone, analysts said.
The reports will be absorbed in trading that ends three hours early -- at 1400 EST/1800 GMT -- ahead of the three-day Presidents Day holiday weekend.
The January Producer Price Index (PPI), due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, is expected to be up 0.3 percent, according to a Reuters poll, after a 0.5 percent December rise.
Without its more volatile food and energy components, the PPI is thought to have risen 0.2 percent in January, after a 0.1 percent December gain.
"If the PPI is OK, as expected, the market certainly could push higher," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury strategist at UBS Securities Inc.
The December business inventories report, due at the same time as the PPI, is expected to show a 0.1 percent decline in inventories is forecast, after a 0.1 percent November rise.
The market is likely to pay little attention to the inventories report, participants said.
"Business inventories are an odd lot as far as adding new information," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
January industrial production data, due at 0915 EST/1415 GMT, are also expected to be benign for the credit market.

Production is expected to be up a slight 0.1 percent after a 0.7 percent December gain. The portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories employed in that production, known as capacity utilization, is forecast at 83.4 percent, off a bit from 83.5 percent in December.
The University of Michigan's preliminary February consumer sentiment index is due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Expectations for that figure center around 97.4.

"The market's mood is upbeat and if the (economic) numbers don't hold any unpleasant surprises, that will allow the market to hold onto the bulk of this week's gains," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.
Karydakis noted the market's ability to rally after the last leg of the Treasury's $39.75 billion refinancing -- the 30-year T-bond auction on Thursday -- drew just tepid demand.

"Despite that, we didn't flinch, and not only that, but we rallied 3/4 of a point after the results were announced," said Karydakis. "Euphoria dominates the marekt and unless stopped by tomorrow's numbers, will persist for a while," he said.
"There was absolutely no concession to the dealer community for this refunding," said Dimick. "That's an impressive performance."
Dimick said "massive liquidity" in the markets right now is affecting stocks, international bonds, as well as U.S. Treasuries."
For now, technical factors are in the market's camp, Dimick said.
"The system is awash in short-term funds," he said. "That means there's a lot of money waiting to be put to work."
Dimick said the March T-bond's push above 113-00 on Thursday would encourage cash to come off the sidelines and into the bond market."
On Thursday, the 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-11/32, up a full point to yield 6.63 percent. The 30-year Treasury bonds auctioned on Thursday ended with a when-issued yield of 6.575 percent.
Fed funds are expected to open at 5-3/16 percent on Friday, dealers indicated.
